answer_text:
Let

\[
f(u)=|\cos(1/u)| \qquad (u\neq 0),
\]

and define \(f(0)\) arbitrarily, since a single point does not affect the integral. Then

\[
F(x)=\int_0^x f(u)\,du,\qquad F(0)=0.
\]

The derivative at \(0\), if it exists, is

\[
F'(0)=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{F(x)-F(0)}{x}
=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac1x\int_0^x |\cos(1/u)|\,du.
\]

Because \(f\) is even, it suffices to compute the right-hand limit \(h\to 0^+\):

\[
\frac{F(h)}{h}=\frac1h\int_0^h |\cos(1/u)|\,du.
\]

Substitute \(t=1/u\), so \(du=-dt/t^2\). Then

\[
\int_0^h |\cos(1/u)|\,du
=\int_{1/h}^{\infty} \frac{|\cos t|}{t^2}\,dt.
\]

Let \(T=1/h\). Then

\[
\frac{F(h)}{h}
= T\int_T^\infty \frac{|\cos t|}{t^2}\,dt.
\]

Now use the average value of \(|\cos t|\) over one period \(\pi\):

\[
\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi |\cos t|\,dt=\frac2\pi.
\]

Write

\[
|\cos t|=\frac2\pi+q(t),
\]

where \(q\) has period \(\pi\) and mean zero. Then

\[
T\int_T^\infty \frac{|\cos t|}{t^2}\,dt
=
T\int_T^\infty \frac{2/\pi}{t^2}\,dt
+
T\int_T^\infty \frac{q(t)}{t^2}\,dt.
\]

The first term is

\[
T\cdot \frac{2/\pi}{T}=\frac2\pi.
\]

For the second term, let

\[
K(t)=\int_0^t q(s)\,ds.
\]

Since \(q\) has zero mean over each period, \(K\) is bounded. Integration by parts gives

\[
\int_T^\infty \frac{q(t)}{t^2}\,dt
=
-\frac{K(T)}{T^2}
+
2\int_T^\infty \frac{K(t)}{t^3}\,dt,
\]

which is \(O(T^{-2})\). Hence

\[
T\int_T^\infty \frac{q(t)}{t^2}\,dt \to 0.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\lim_{h\to 0^+}\frac{F(h)}{h}=\frac2\pi.
\]

By evenness of the integrand, the left-hand limit is the same:

\[
\lim_{h\to 0^+}\frac{F(-h)}{-h}
=
\lim_{h\to 0^+}\frac1h\int_0^h |\cos(1/u)|\,du
=
\frac2\pi.
\]

Thus the derivative exists at \(0\), and

\[
\boxed{F'(0)=\frac{2}{\pi}}.
\]

27B·v4.method: Substitution t=1/u converts the average to a weighted integral; the period-mean of |cos t| (2/π) gives the leading asymptotic term.
